newsitem.title: USA: Raising kids with just a little cash.
newsitem.headline: Raising kids with just a little cash.

text.p: Lisa Reid, a sexual abuse counsellor in Santa Fe, New Mexico, wanted to be home with her two children, oversee their education, and save money rather than earn it.
She and her husband, Jim, formerly a mechanical engineer, decided to set up their lives so they could save money and be able to have more options -- "live your life your way, doing work you love."
This required an "attitude switch," Reid said from her home, and presented "a whole new way of thinking."
Her experiences resulted in the new book, "Raising Kids With Just a Little Cash" (Ferguson-Carol Publishers, $14.95).

"I'm not into deprivation," she said, but when she explained the life style switch to her daughters, now six and 11, "I had to make it really clear that we were taking these actions so Dad would be more available to the kids."
She said, "the kids had a really clear idea that certain actions made life changes possible."
Living frugally but living well takes a lot of time, and to Reid, time is money.
She said that she spends "$10 to $15 a week" on researching her money savings activities, such as coupon clipping and scanning papers for discounts.

In her "time is money saved formula," Reid said that by determining how much per hour you are "spending" on various activities, you can make choices about where to put your energy, hopefully in the most cost-effective ways.

Reid belives that her cost-savings activities have saved her $165 a week for about 11 hours of work. According to her calculations, adding in child care, transportation, clothes and meals out, she would have to earn $16,312 a year, or $28.50 an hour, to take home an amount equal to what she saved.

"I saw that stopping at one more store just to buy tuna on sale was worth $20 for 15 minutes (or the equivalent of a $100 gross hourly wage) when I bought 48 cans at once -- not a waste of time after all," she writes.
After all, she said, the average working mother earns $9 an hour working outside the home.

Reid found, however, that the 70 cents an hour she saves on hanging her laundry on the line to dry was not good economics. Putting the laundry in the dryer left her with enough energy to cook dinner from scratch, which saved her $5 to $7 an hour compared with using ready prepared foods.
Reid said that money saving activities include buying food in bulk, saving often 10 percent to 20 percent if buying a case at a time.

She buys her family's clothes, which can be a major expense, at thrift stores and yard sales. She also gladly accepts hand-me-downs. The rare items she buys at department stores, in bulk and when on sale, include underwear and socks.

Thinking creatively is also a money saving activity. For children's birthday parties, which at the local play gym or pizzaria/video parlour can set families back a bundle, she suggests some creative activities such as making puppets, decorating T-shirts, treasure hunts, face painting or even going to view a local farm team or semi-pro baseball game.
One thing she won't skimp on is health. Reid said she advocates buying major medical insurance, for under $100 a month, but suggests that parents "learn to manage minor illness on your own."

Much of family health revolves around good nutrition, she says, homeopathic and herbal remedies and "good common sense" including accident prevention. However, "if my child has a trauma, like a broken arm, or a potentially life-threatening illness, I head for a health professional."
Reid's life style change has allowed her husband, now a massage therapist, to spend more time at home.
"Most families are totally stretched for time and money," she said, but believes that her efforts "have other values you can't put a money value on."
Reid has also started a newsletter, PurseStrings -- for famililies who want to spend less and enjoy more.
